implementerProof.whatTheProofDidNotCover: I could not establish the review's duration claim for the scenario I drove. Its finding says a refused notification leaves the reader on stale text 'until that document is written again'; at the pre-fix tree the same burst recovered in about six seconds, twice over, by some other path — most likely the room's own settlement meeting the durable gate and failing the room, though I did not isolate it. So my control below is 2.0 s against 6.0 s, not 2.0 s against never. The fix is still the right one and the shorter, explicit path; I have not shown the pre-fix hold is unbounded, and I am not implying it.

proof.criterion: The review's important finding: the trailing write of a burst on the other process must not leave a connected reader holding text the store has replaced. A room with a browser in it never reaches roomIdleTimeout, so the interval's refusal has to be re-examined rather than dropped.
proof.surface: Two real envoy-dispatch processes on one Postgres 17 and one nats-server 2.10 in this issue's pod, with a real document websocket client holding the room on A and the burst made through B's HTTP API: the first write evicts and the browser reconnects, and the second lands inside the two-second eviction interval that the first one started, so its notification is one the interval refuses.
proof.command: cd packages/envoy && . /legion/harness/env.sh && go test -tags multiprocess -count=1 -timeout 15m -run TestProbeTheTrailingWriteOfABurstDoesNotLeaveAReaderOnStaleText ./cmd/dispatch   (throwaway probe, removed before this handoff)
proof.observed: The trailing write landed 94 ms after the first eviction, well inside the interval, and the room closed 1.995 s after that write — the window's own length, which is the deferred re-examination and not a fresh notification, since nothing wrote the document again. Both processes then served the stored text ("after").
proof.negativeControl: Driven on a scratch clone at the pre-fix tree (555a7e363191, the review handoff's commit) with the same probe: the room closed 6.03 s and 6.02 s after the trailing write on two runs, against 1.995 s here. So the control is a measured difference in the path and its latency, not closes-against-never — at the pre-fix tree something else recovered the room in about six seconds, and I did not isolate what. An intermediate control is in the same record: with only the wake unwired (NextWake/OnWake removed from the listener, the sweep on reconnect left in place) the room closed 6.03 s after the write, which is what identifies the 2.0 s path as the deferral specifically.
